name: Sensitivity Point
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Lever That Moves One Dial: Identifying Sensitivity Points
lesson.summary: A sensitivity point is an architectural decision that strongly affects one quality attribute, and finding these decisions is how an ATAM evaluation locates the design choices that most deserve scrutiny.
lesson.body:
Once a utility tree has surfaced the highest priority quality attribute scenarios, an ATAM team traces each scenario through the actual architecture to see which design decisions determine whether the response is achieved. A sensitivity point is a property of the architecture, a single decision or parameter, that has a strong effect on one particular quality attribute response. Change that decision even a little, and the scenario's outcome changes noticeably. Sensitivity points are how an evaluation moves from abstract quality attributes back to specific, nameable choices an architect actually made.

Bitcoin's block interval, targeted at ten minutes through a difficulty adjustment algorithm, is a clean sensitivity point for confirmation latency. Shorten the target interval and average confirmation time for a given number of confirmations drops; lengthen it and confirmation time rises. The relationship is direct and largely isolated to that one quality attribute, which is exactly what marks a decision as a sensitivity point rather than something more diffuse. The number of validators required to finalize a block in a proof of stake system is a similar sensitivity point for the availability scenario covering validator outages: requiring signatures from a very high fraction of validators makes finality strongly sensitive to any subset of validators going offline.

Finding sensitivity points is valuable precisely because they identify where a small architectural change buys a large improvement, or a small architectural mistake causes a large regression, in one quality attribute. A review team that has traced the ten thousand simultaneous transaction scenario from the utility tree back through the architecture might find the block gas limit, the parameter capping how much computation fits in a single block, is the sensitivity point governing whether that scenario's throughput response measure is met. Raise the gas limit and more transactions fit per block; the scenario's outcome moves accordingly.

Sensitivity points are not inherently good or bad. Identifying one is simply identifying leverage: a place where the architecture's behavior on a given quality attribute is concentrated in a single decision rather than distributed across many. What sensitivity points do not yet tell the review team is what else that same decision affects. A gas limit that is a sensitivity point for throughput might also, quietly, be a sensitivity point for the cost of running a full node, since larger blocks mean more data every node must download and store. When one architectural decision turns up as a sensitivity point for two quality attributes that move in opposite directions, ATAM has a name for that, and it is the subject of the next chapter.

A single scenario can also have more than one sensitivity point worth recording separately. The availability scenario about a coordinated validator exit, for example, is sensitive both to the finality threshold discussed above and, independently, to how quickly the protocol lets new validators join to replace those who left. Listing both, rather than collapsing them into one vague note about validator churn, is what lets an ATAM report tell an architect exactly which two dials to examine, instead of leaving them to guess where in a large codebase the real leverage actually sits.
